SEBoK Life Cycle Model Overview, Distilled

Fifth-batch SEBoK distillation, batch 2/5 doc 6 (SE-173). The named Life Cycle Model Overview page resolves to the Life Cycle Models page (overview content). The page is the canonical Cluster I (pin-art / temporal-concurrency) cadence-lattice anchor at the lifecycle-model rung: it explicitly enumerates multiple cadence types (waterfall sequential, incremental, evolutionary iterative, DevOps infinity-loop continuous-without-handoff) and articulates the four core principles of life-cycle modeling. Cadence-lattice (§VII.6 candidate, §VII.7 formalization-strong) anchors here at maximum strength: the page itself is the cadence-axis enumeration. The four core principles (stages-of-existence × supporting-systems × quality-characteristics-by-stage × stage-criteria) are a Cluster A four-axis universal-sibling lattice at the life-cycle-model-axiom rung. The "infinity loop" DevOps reference is the continuous-without-handoff terminal cadence (anchoring SE-168). "Concurrently, iteratively, and recursively" is reproduced verbatim — SE-044 anchor binding. Six clusters compose; cadence-lattice (Cluster I) reaches its strongest single-page anchor in the fifth-batch sweep.

II. Source Read

Definition: a life cycle model is "a framework of processes and activities concerned with the life cycle which can be organized into stages" (ISO/IEC/IEEE 24748-1:2024). Four core principles: (1) systems progress through defined stages during their existence, (2) supporting systems must be available to achieve each stage's outcomes, (3) quality characteristics (producibility, usability, supportability, disposability) should be specified at appropriate stages, (4) stages begin and end based on specific criteria or external events. Model characteristics: some permit "iteration and concurrency of stages"; a system can occupy multiple lifecycle stages simultaneously. Common model types referenced: waterfall, incremental, evolutionary; some referenced as "project models, not life cycle models." DevOps reference, verbatim: "One alternative model depicts lifecycle stages in an infinity loop where there is no distinction between development and support phases, assuming minimal retirement considerations." Life-cycle processes are activities integrated into models, often applied "concurrently, iteratively, and recursively" across lifecycle stages.

Cluster B (multi-keeper) at quality-characteristics-by-stage axiom. Quality characteristics specified "at appropriate stages" reads as multi-keeper composition where each stage-keeper composes against the system-stage substrate, and the integration produces the temporally-keyed quality-characteristic specification. Convergent with §VII.7 three-scale Cluster B; SE-173 supplies a temporal-axis Cluster B instance.

Cluster F (longitudinal-pulverization, SE-114) at stage-progression rung. "Systems progress through defined stages during their existence" is canonical Cluster F at the lifecycle-stage pulverization rung. Convergent with SE-114's longitudinal-pulverization formalization at IM anchor; SE-173 is the parent-rung anchor for stage-pulverization.

Cluster J (engineered-system context) at "system can occupy multiple stages simultaneously" sub-instance. The page's claim that a system can occupy multiple lifecycle stages simultaneously is a Cluster J reading: the engineered-system unit of analysis is preserved while stage-occupancy multiplexes. Worth flagging: this is the canonical temporal-multiplexing Cluster J sub-instance.

Cluster I "concurrently, iteratively, and recursively" reproduced verbatim. SE-044 anchor formulation appears at the parent rung. Both anchors (SE-044 process-rung + SE-173 lifecycle-model-rung) bind Cluster I at adjacent rungs.
